entities.summary:
The Mahābhārata, an ancient Indian epic composed around the 4th century BCE to the 4th century CE, stands as a monumental text in Hindu literature and philosophy. Spanning the narrative of the Kurukshetra War between the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, it reflects the complexities of dharma (duty/righteousness) and has influenced spiritual and ethical thought across centuries. This epic, attributed to the sage Vyasa, not only narrates a grand tale but also encompasses diverse themes including governance, justice, and morality, making it a cornerstone of Indian culture and identity.

The epic unfolds through a myriad of sub-stories, including the Bhagavad Gita, which presents a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and the god Krishna on the battlefield, symbolizing the struggle between duty and ethics. Spanning over 100,000 verses, it serves both as a narrative and a philosophical treatise, discussing the four puruṣārthas (goals of life): dharma, artha (prosperity), kāma (pleasure), and moksha (liberation). The Mahābhārata's composition reflects a synthesis of various oral traditions and regional narratives, contributing significantly to the cultural and spiritual landscape of South Asia.

The legacy of the Mahābhārata extends beyond its narrative as it has been a source of inspiration for countless adaptations in literature, art, and performance across Asia. It has influenced political thought and social structures, particularly in the context of Hindu kingship and governance. The themes of the epic resonate in contemporary discussions on ethics and morality, showcasing its relevance in modern society. Moreover, various retellings and reinterpretations have allowed for its continued presence in global culture, establishing it as a pivotal work of literature.
